story_text.value:
A "deepswapp" of a website has data from one website in a layout of another website. Deepswapp Browser allows users to seamlessly browse this alternative version of the Internet, today.

Video: https://deepswapp.com/assets/deepswapp.mp4

The whole Web can look like Wikipedia, old Reddit, or your own website. Once deepswapped, the website transformation is reusable without AI.

    Single-file HTML page
    Only essential data rendered
    Synchronized tabs
    Synchronized scrolling
    No backgrounds
    No animations
    Data auto-refresh
    Image lazy loading
This desktop app works on every platform (Docker images also available) and opens a separate Chrome instance, which mirrors opened tabs in the user's main browser. Several deepswapps are included with the download, so no AI subscription is needed for a test drive. A fresh deepswapp takes around 10 minutes and costs about $0.40c on deepseek-v4.1-flash. This goes down by half when deepswapping a known website.

Tech side: fully in Golang, with AI-generated JavaScript never executing in the user's main browser.

Roadmap: Web and Mobile access, even deeper swaps, parallel swaps.

https://deepswapp.com

title.value: Show HN: Deepswapp Browser: browser the browser with another browser

story_text.value:
For the busy people out there, the GitHub repo has a demo video so you can see if this is worth your time: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

The video was created by Opus 5.5; I just asked it to create a demo video (it has a 'record' tool), so I think this is a good idea of how well it can work with the tool.

---

pw-repl is a tool that makes it easy for you and your agents to work with Playwright+CDP in a browser (your current headed session, or a headless one, or both at the same time; take your pick).

It's basically a Playwright-powered swiss army knife that helps you and agents poke around your browser: Try out different features of a website, break things (e.g. mock backend responses), take screenshots, record videos, etc.

The GitHub repo shows a video, recorded by an agent using pw-repl: https://github.com/arcanemachine/pw-repl

One cool thing it can do: create videos of bug reports. You can tell an agent about a bug and to use pw-repl to capture it, and it can record a video with the built-in toast feature to narrate its actions, and show a virtual mouse to simulate actions on the screen, as if it were a user. It's also useful for capturing screenshots (which can be combined with the toast and highlight tools to emphasize certain elements or information), and has many useful features that can help agents to use it efficiently.

This isn't intended to be commercialized in any way. It's just a neat tool that I (with Claude's help) cobbled together. It's completely vibe-coded, and is intended mainly as a debugging aid. I use all the time, and hope it may be helpful for others.

It's basically just Playwright + CDP under the hood, but has some extra tools and an interface that make it easier for agents to work with.

The quickest way to try it out is to tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background --launch`, which starts a headless Chromium of its own. No browser setup needed. (If you don't like such `curl | bash`-esque installation instructions, read the code, or get your agent to take a look at it.)

To use it in your own browser instead, start Chrome with CDP enabled (`chrome --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir="$HOME/.config/chrome-debug"`), and tell your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest serve --background`. (The separate `--user-data-dir` is needed because recent versions of Chrome don't open the debugging port on your default profile.)

It also can generate a skill so that you can just run `/pw-repl do some stuff`. Get your agent to run `npx pw-repl@latest skill > <skills folder>/pw-repl/SKILL.md` (e.g. `~/.claude/skills/pw-repl/SKILL.md` for Claude Code).

NOTE: This has only been tested on my Linux machine, so not sure if it will work on macOS. It should, but I haven't tried it out personally.

Fun fact: This tool was originally a random REPL that Claude generated on-the-fly to do some random thing. I saw it and was blown away, so I got Claude to make it into its own application. I suspect that Claude may have taken "inspiration" from an existing project with a similar name, so credit where credit is due to this other `playwright-repl` package: https://github.com/stevez/playwright-repl

title.value: Show HN: pw-repl - A Playwright-powered REPL for you and your agents to share

story_text.value:
Hi, I want to share with you my chrome extension: Tabverse, as it is now passed the reveiw of Chrome Web Store and live at: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/tabverse/lffblcippn...

Tabverse is a local first workona like chrome extension for managing tabs, with its source open at https://www.github.com/liyu1981/tabverse.

In essential it has the core functions workona has, but can operate totally locally, which means it will not need an account nor subscription. The only limit is your local storage spaces so that you can have as many spaces(I call tabverse) as you can. It is open source, so not just your data stays with you, and the tool itself will stay with you in future.

Beyond the normal workona features (persisted workspace, load/reload/import/export, note/bookmark/history tools), there are features does require a server. Features like backup/sync, global search on all tabverses, and future collaboration (not yet done), can only be possible if there is a server. I build this part in open too: the server is free to self host and open source in same repo of Tabverse.

The tabverse's idea was with me few years ago while I was using Workona and was frustrated with its limitation on free tier (remember was only 5 workspaces), and the missing features of managing multiple workspaces at the same time. Tabverse takes the idea of Workona, and develop further: each window with a Tabverse tab is a workspace, all stored in local storage, and multi windows can have multi Tabverses same time, and can switch fast. There can even be window without Tabverse, so besides work, personal stuff or entertainment will have place to go. As I build this alone, in the middle, almost give up on this project, and luckily AI agents now is there: not only I have a good helper, but also I have a partner I can discuss a bit. So this time the first version starts with v0.7.2.

But AI agent can never replace the real need from human on what should be built and what works better, so I want to share with you and listen to your feedbacks early. Please give it a try, and every feedback to me is a gift.

Besides the self-hosted option, I host a server at https://tabverse.liyu1981.xyz (yes, the same website of intro and docs), but is invitation only. If you want to help me to test in this early stage, you can login with Google (the only social login I configured :)), and request an invitation there. I will act as soon as I find your request :). But do not worry at all if you only want to use Tabverse locally without a server -- that is the first thing when I was building it.

In current version there are also AI features built in, and again do not worry as the AI features is using Chrome's Prompt API, which is totally local, with Gemini Nano (first time will need to download it automatically), nothing send to a server, and you can always turn this on of off in settings. Morden computers with decent memory should work well, but some older computer may suffer (so please turn off). And it is Chrome only. (Honestly, Tabverse currently only support Google Chrome, but not other Chrome based browsers).

title.value: Show HN: Tabverse – a free, open-source, with self-hostable server Workona clone

story_text.value:
This question has been bugging me for a while: do different AI models have a different design sense? Does it matter which one I pick?

I built UI Palooza to explore that. I gave models the same four frontend briefs, with enough room to choose their own typography, colors, layouts, and interactions. Then I repeated the runs with different design skills and sample directions.

The public collection has 1,784 designs. You can compare them side by side and open the working websites, not just screenshots. No signup required.

One way to explore it: pick a brief and Baseline A, then compare Vanilla with a design skill. Or keep the skill fixed and look across models.

I’d be interested in which patterns you notice—and what you’d change about the experiment.

title.value: Show HN: UIPalooza – Do AI models have a recognizable design taste?

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we're Mike and Thom.

Agents of the future should only have one tool (the interpreter, ideally a LISP eval), nothing more or less; to interact with the world. Agents remember by writing markdown files. NODECODE remembers by rewriting itself. And that is in itself a new paradigm in working with agents. What if memories, skills, MCPs, provider connectors, tools, etc. all live under the same image as *.lisp files instead of in disarray across random folders?

Ask it for something it can’t do, and it writes what it needs into its OWN running image and keeps it even after a restart. (Changes in a LISP image have significantly lower ceremony and overhead than in harnesses written in other languages):

Small intuitive scenario:

> you can't read PDFs. teach yourself. (defun read-pdf (path) ...) ; runs at once, kept (read-pdf "invoices/0421.pdf") ;; Globex owes $1,240.00, due Oct 24, unpaid. [… rest of PDF content]

read-pdf is still there after a restart, in your terminal, and in every other UI clients (Discord, web app, etc.)

Technically at a lower level; NODECODE runs as one process in SBCL, a Common Lisp system, and shells attach to it. The model has one tool: it evaluates LISP in the running program. Code is data, so a program can rewrite itself while it runs. What the model defines runs at once and is kept, one file per definition, committed with git, loaded at every start.

Why LISP now? Current SOTA models have reached an optimum point in how they efficiently work with LISP, though not as fluently as Python. Still, we believe AGI will understand ANY language (past/present/future) by understanding the crux of any given language, and not through excessive and expensive pretraining scheme.

Why LISP in general? We believe LISP is the current language that communicates to the world with the least bandwidth.

Why another LISP agent? The LISP harnesses we found are hard to use unless you already know the language itself, and so we had this idea of simplifying and condensing the UX to be user friendly for the masses, while leveraging the power of LISP. Code as data is what lets an agent change itself, and that shouldn't need a LISP hacker to run. NODECODE is our first step toward putting it on everyone's PC and mobile. You ask in plain words, the model writes LISP, and you get briefed in natural language; that is how it should be.

Extensions? Code as data also suits extensions. We see NODECODE as a living agent organism. To us, it feels very much alive, and so this brings us to the Cells system. A Cell is a folder that teaches NODECODE something new: a chat room it can live in (e.g Discord, Telegram, Slack, etc. - Yes we made Cells for channels to have it act as a very capable personal agent), a skill, a memory, MCPs, new tools, etc. Install one from our Cell hub or ask it to write a custom, personalized one. Either way it is more code the agent can read and change.

Your terminal, a browser tab, your phone and bots in Discord, Telegram and Slack all attach to that SAME gateway process, so a tool it writes in one is there in ALL of them. Over time it becomes yours and it is continuously evolving; the organism within it; NODECODE.

MIT License. https://github.com/nodecode-ai/nodecode X/twitter/demo launch post: https://x.com/pomterree/status/2113721985167728757 docs: https://nodecode.ai/docs

title.value: Show HN: Nodecode, open-source living agent in Lisp that rewrites itself for you
